system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2135-04-27 18:36:00 to 2135-04-28 15:06:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of chronic bilateral rotator cuff tears, septic arthritis of the left shoulder, aortic stenosis, and SIADH was admitted for worsening right shoulder pain radiating down the arm, swelling, and limited mobility. He had been managing pain with Tylenol and Tramadol, but symptoms had become intolerable. Imaging showed severe degenerative joint disease and rotator cuff tear, unchanged from prior studies. Arthrocentesis was performed, and joint fluid analysis revealed no infection, with no organisms seen on gram stain and no growth in culture. Inflammatory markers were only mildly elevated. Pain was managed with oxycodone initially, then transitioned with the addition of short-course ibuprofen. Hyponatremia remained stable on a normal diet with added salt. The patient improved clinically, with reduced pain and swelling, and was discharged home on a plan to continue pain medications, complete a three-day course of ibuprofen, and follow up with primary care and orthopedics.
problems: Disorders of bursae and tendons in shoulder region, unspecified
Osteoarthrosis, localized, not specified whether primary or secondary, shoulder region
Personal history of peptic ulcer disease

diagnoses.long_title: Other accident caused by striking against or being struck accidentally by objects or persons

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you were hit in the head during physical therapy earlier today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. A therapy ball struck me on the side of the head. I saw flashes and thought I was going blind—but I’m nearly blind already, so it’s hard to tell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The ER did a CT scan of your head to check for any bleeding or injury. Good news—it shows no acute problems like a bleed or fracture. Just some stable changes from aging and small vessel disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. But I’ve been feeling weak and nauseous. I haven’t been eating well since my UTI treatment last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your labs show two main issues. Your sodium is low—121, which is a bit below your usual baseline of 125. And your kidney function is temporarily impaired, with creatinine up to 1.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? My son said my blood pressure was high earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The low sodium and kidney issue are likely due to not eating or drinking well, plus you mentioned being on a low-salt diet by accident. That can worsen hyponatremia, especially with your history of SIADH.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, yes. The nursing home switched my meals. I didn’t realize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you a liter of normal saline. That’s already helped—your sodium improved to 127, and your creatinine dropped to 1.0. So your kidneys are responding well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But will I need more fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’re stable now. We’ll just ask you to limit extra water and go back to your regular salt intake. No more low-salt diet. That should keep your sodium steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure? It’s been high lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bit elevated at 168 over 92, but not alarming. We’ll continue your home medications—metoprolol and losartan—to keep it controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your repeat labs. Your sodium is holding at 127, and kidney function remains improved. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. Can I go back to the care facility today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you this morning. We’ll update your medications slightly—lower dose of metoprolol and simvastatin, and we’re adding ranitidine for stomach protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tramadol for shoulder pain? I still need that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue tramadol and acetaminophen as needed. Also keep using your eye drops and constipation meds—docusate and senna.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I should keep taking aspirin every day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the chewable aspirin daily is important for heart protection, especially with your history. Just avoid ibuprofen or other NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. And my dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing meclizine three times a day for that. Make sure you get up slowly and use your walker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have the discharge papers ready soon. Your son will help you get back to the extended care facility safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. Any new symptoms—headache, nausea, or vision changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none. Just ready to go back to my routine.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of SIADH, hypertension, aortic stenosis, and chronic bilateral rotator cuff tears was admitted after being struck in the head with a ball during physical therapy. He reported transient visual changes but had no headache or neurological deficits. Initial labs revealed acute hyponatremia (Na 121) and acute renal failure (creatinine 1.5), likely due to poor oral intake and accidental low-salt diet. A non-contrast head CT showed no acute intracranial injury. He received one liter of normal saline, which improved sodium to 127 and creatinine to 1.0. His blood pressure was managed with continued home antihypertensives. He remained stable, with no complications, and was discharged to an extended care facility on a revised medication list including ranitidine for GI protection and continued management of chronic conditions.
